name: DepositRootStorageArgumentReadAfterLaterArguments
summary: ``depositroot`` reads a storage ``bytes`` argument only after evaluating the later arguments, so a side effect of a later argument changes the data it hashes, while the SMTChecker assumes the data as it was when the argument was evaluated.
description: Both code generators encode the arguments of ``depositroot`` after evaluating all of them, so a storage ``bytes`` argument is copied to memory only then. If a later argument modifies that storage, for example through a function call, ``depositroot`` hashes the modified data. The SMTChecker records the value of each argument when it is evaluated, so it can prove a property about the unmodified data that fails at run time. Optimizer settings have no influence.

name: ReturndatacopyWithStaleSizeRemoved
summary: The Yul optimizer can remove a ``returndatacopy`` whose length is the result of an earlier ``returndatasize()`` call even after another call has changed the return data, so a copy that has to revert does not.
description: The ``UnusedStoreEliminator`` optimizer step removes stores whose result is never read. It treats ``returndatacopy(destination, 0, size)`` as removable when ``size`` holds the result of a ``returndatasize()`` call, because such a copy cannot revert. If another external call runs between the ``returndatasize()`` call and the copy and returns less data, the copy has to revert, and removing it lets execution continue. Only inline assembly or stand-alone Yul that keeps the result of ``returndatasize()`` across another call and never reads the copied memory is affected. The compiler does not generate this pattern itself. Unoptimized code is unaffected.

name: UnsetPackedInternalFunctionPointerJumpsToZero
summary: In the legacy code generator, calling an internal function pointer in storage that was never assigned fails with an invalid jump that consumes all gas passed to the call, instead of reverting with ``Panic(0x51)``, if a non-zero value is packed after it in the same storage slot.
description: When the legacy code generator reads an internal function pointer from storage, it replaces a zero value with a function that reverts with ``Panic(0x51)``. It tests for zero before masking the pointer out of its storage slot, so a non-zero value packed after the pointer in the same slot makes the test fail. The masked pointer is then zero, and calling it jumps to code offset 0, which is not a jump destination. The call fails as an invalid instruction would: it consumes all gas passed to it and returns no error data. Storage is not changed. The IR code generator is not affected. Optimizer settings have no influence. Fixed on the development branch by masking the packed pointer before zero detection; regression tests exercise both pipelines with nonzero neighbours, assigned pointers and deleted pointers.

name: ConstantEvaluatedInFirstUseArithmeticMode
summary: The IR code generator compiles the initializer of a ``constant`` once, in the checked or ``unchecked`` arithmetic mode of the first place that reads it, and every other read reuses that code.
description: The IR code generator turns each ``constant`` whose initializer is not evaluated at compile time into a single Yul function, generated the first time the constant is read and in the arithmetic mode in effect at that read. If the first read is inside an ``unchecked`` block, an initializer that overflows wraps for every read, so a checked read silently wraps instead of reverting with ``Panic(0x11)``. If the first read is checked, including the public getter, which is generated first, an ``unchecked`` read reverts with ``Panic(0x11)``. The legacy code generator is not affected. Optimizer settings have no influence.

name: LegacyUint256DirtyUpperBits
summary: In the legacy code generator, a ``uint256`` or ``int256`` value produced by a narrowing conversion, a sign conversion or wrapping ``unchecked`` arithmetic can keep bits 256 to 511 of the 512-bit VM word set, and ``addmod``, ``mulmod``, inline assembly, ``new``, slice bounds and call options use those bits.
description: The legacy code generator cleans the high-order bits of values narrower than the VM word only where it uses them in comparisons, shifts, and memory or storage writes. In Solidity this is sound for ``uint256`` and ``int256``, because they fill the 256-bit EVM word. From 0.2.0 the QRVM word is 512 bits wide while ``uint256`` and ``int256`` remain 256-bit types, and the legacy code generator does not clean bits 256 to 511 where Solidity never had to. A value produced by an explicit narrowing such as ``uint256(x)`` with ``x`` a ``uint512``, by a sign conversion such as ``uint256(int256(-1))``, or by ``unchecked`` addition, subtraction or multiplication that wraps keeps bits 256 to 511. ``addmod`` and ``mulmod`` then compute with the 512-bit value and return wrong results. Inline assembly reads the 512-bit value, and ``mstore`` writes it in full. ``new bytes(n)`` and ``new T[](n)`` revert with ``Panic(0x41)``, slice bounds checks revert, and ``{value: ...}`` and ``{gas: ...}`` call options make the call fail. The IR code generator cleans these values and is not affected, so the two pipelines can compile the same source to different results. Optimizer settings have no influence. On the development branch, allocation lengths, slice bounds, the parameters of addmod and mulmod, and call value and gas options now use full-word uint, so passing a uint256 value to these consumers widens and cleans it. Inline assembly continues to require explicit cleanup of narrow values as documented in assembly.rst. Legacy retains cleanup at use for all integer types narrower than 512 bits. Dirty upper bits after narrowing or unchecked arithmetic are not themselves a miscompilation; typed consumers must preserve the declared width.

name: YulOptimizerKnowledgeBaseStaleBookkeeping
summary: The Yul optimizer could consider two memory or storage locations distinct even though their addresses were computed from different values of the same reassigned variable and coincided at runtime. This could lead to loads being replaced with outdated values and to needed stores being removed.
description: The Yul optimizer steps ``LoadResolver`` and ``EqualStoreEliminator`` keep track of what was stored in memory and storage. ``LoadResolver`` uses this to replace loads and ``keccak256`` calls with known values, and ``EqualStoreEliminator`` uses it to remove stores of a value that the location already contains. Whenever a store is encountered whose exact location cannot be determined, the optimizer has to forget what it knows about every location the store might overwrite. To decide this, the optimizer represents an address symbolically as a constant offset either from zero or from another variable, its base variable. Two addresses with the same base can then be determined to be distinct if their offsets differ (for storage) or are at least one VM word apart (for memory). These representations are cached per variable. The base variable, however, may be reassigned afterwards. The optimizer does not always notice and then compares an address computed from the old value of the base with an address computed from the new value as if both used the same base. As a result, it can consider two locations distinct even though they coincide at runtime, keeping a stale entry for a location that has just been overwritten. A subsequent load from that location can then be replaced with an outdated value, a subsequent store of that value to the location can be removed, and ``keccak256`` over the location can be replaced with the hash of an outdated value. Whether the bug is triggered depends on the structure of the intermediate code these optimizer steps receive. It is therefore sensitive to the optimizer sequence and to the surrounding code, and the two locations additionally have to coincide at runtime. In optimized IR code generation, any code may be affected, including code without inline assembly. In optimized legacy code generation, only inline assembly that does not refer to any Hyperion variables or functions and compiler-generated Yul utility functions could be affected. Unoptimized code is unaffected. Inherited from Solidity 0.8.23: upstream SOL-2026-7, fixed in Solidity 0.8.38.

name: VerifierStorageArgumentCopiedAfterLaterArguments
summary: The IR code generator copies a storage ``bytes`` argument of ``mldsa87verify`` or ``xmssverify`` to memory only after evaluating the later arguments, so a side effect of a later argument changes the data passed to the precompile.
description: The IR code generator evaluates every argument of ``mldsa87verify`` and ``xmssverify`` before converting any of them to its parameter type, so a storage ``bytes`` argument is copied to memory only after the later arguments have been evaluated. If a later argument modifies that storage, for example through a function call that overwrites a stored signature, the precompile receives the modified data. The legacy code generator and the SMTChecker convert each argument right after evaluating it and use the data as it was, so legacy and IR builds of the same source can give different results, and properties the SMTChecker proves can fail at run time. Optimizer settings have no influence.

name: MemoryByteArrayElementDeleteClearsWholeWord
summary: Applying ``delete`` to a single element of a ``bytes`` array in memory clears not only that element but the whole VM word starting at the element's location, zeroing up to 63 bytes beyond the element, or 31 bytes up to 0.1.0.
description: Elements of ``bytes`` arrays in memory are packed, each occupying a single byte. When a value is assigned to such an element, the legacy code generator correctly stores it with a single-byte ``MSTORE8`` instruction. The code path in the legacy code generator implementing ``delete`` on such an element, however, writes the zero value with a full-word ``MSTORE``, clearing the 64 bytes starting at the element's location, or 32 bytes up to 0.1.0, when the QRVM word was 256 bits wide. The bytes following the element within the array are silently zeroed. If the element is within the last 63 bytes of the array's allocation, or the last 31 bytes up to 0.1.0, the write also extends past it into the area where the allocator places the next memory object, clearing the most significant bytes of that object's first word. How many elements are in reach depends on the size of the allocation: arrays created with ``new bytes(n)`` or from literals occupy their length rounded up to a multiple of the word size, so only elements falling within the last word-size-minus-one bytes of that rounded-up area, if any, can be affected. The results of ``bytes.concat``, ``string.concat``, and the ``abi.encode*`` functions, on the other hand, are placed by the legacy code generator in an allocation of exactly the size of their data, so the next object starts immediately after their last element and each of their last 63 elements, or 31 up to 0.1.0, is in reach. Assigning zero to an element (``b[i] = 0``) is not affected, only the ``delete`` operator, and neither are byte arrays in storage or calldata. The bug exists only in the legacy code generator. Code compiled via IR is unaffected. Optimizer settings have no influence. Inherited from Solidity 0.8.23: upstream SOL-2026-5, fixed in Solidity 0.8.37.

name: SpillSlotCollisionAcrossMutualRecursion
summary: Local variables of two simultaneously active functions moved to fixed memory offsets by the stack limit evader may be assigned the same offset if the call graph contains mutual recursion, so that one variable is silently overwritten by the other.
description: To work around the 16-slot stack access limit of the QRVM, the IR-based code generator can, under some preconditions, move local variables to fixed memory offsets. Variables that can never be active at the same time may safely share an offset, so the reserved memory area is sized by a depth-first walk of the call graph that computes for every node the number of slots it and its callees need. To keep this walk from descending infinitely into recursive call chains, the slot count is initialized with zero upon entering it. This provisional zero is observable: a function reached again through a call graph cycle reports an empty footprint to its caller, the caller's count is finalized and cached on that basis, and the undercount propagates to every later caller, including functions outside the cycle. As a result, a function called by such a cycle and a function calling into it can be assigned the same memory slot even though both can be active at the same time. A relocated variable still needed after the call into the cycle returns has then been silently overwritten by the called function, producing wrong results. Triggering the bug requires the IR pipeline and a call graph in which a cycle of at least two mutually recursive functions both reaches a function needing relocation of variables to memory and is entered from a separate call chain whose own relocated variable is read again after the call towards the cycle returns. It is independent of whether the optimizer is enabled. Inherited from Solidity 0.8.23: upstream SOL-2026-4, fixed in Solidity 0.8.37.

name: UnsoundSpillInMutualRecursion
summary: Local variables of a function involved in mutual recursion may spuriously be moved to fixed memory offsets and overwritten across recursive calls.
description: To work around the 16-slot stack access limit of the QRVM, the IR-based code generator can move local variables of stack-too-deep functions to fixed memory offsets. This relocation is unsound for recursive functions: a fixed offset would be shared by all activations of the function, so a recursive call would overwrite the caller's value. The stack limit evader therefore must not relocate variables of functions that are part of a recursive call chain. To this end, the call graph is searched for cycles using a path-based depth-first search that, once a function has been fully explored and popped from the search path, short-circuits on it on any later visit. As a result, a function shared between several intersecting cycles can be reached first through a path that does not yet close a cycle through it, get marked as finished, and then be skipped when a later path would have revealed that it does lie on a cycle. Such a function is misclassified as non-recursive. When a misclassified function is complex enough for the stack limit evader to relocate some of its variables, those variables are moved to fixed memory offsets and silently corrupted on recursion, producing wrong results rather than a compile-time error. Triggering the bug requires the IR pipeline, a set of mutually recursive functions whose call graph contains intersecting cycles, at least one of the functions in an undetected part of a cycle being complex enough to require relocation to memory, and an unfortunate processing order of the functions, which depends on the hashes of their Yul names. It is independent of whether the optimizer is enabled. Inherited from Solidity 0.8.23: upstream SOL-2026-2, fixed in Solidity 0.8.36.

name: LostStorageArrayWriteOnSlotOverflow
summary: Operations that involve clearing or copying from arrays that straddle the end of storage could result in silent data retention.
description: Hyperion makes it possible to define variables that extend past the last slot of storage, which results in wrap-around back to slot zero. The last slot is 2**256 - 1 up to 0.1.0 and 2**512 - 1 from 0.2.0, when the QRVM word became 512 bits wide. Since the QRVM wraps integer arithmetic at the word size, most operations on such variables just work. The only situation which requires special attention is iteration against absolute slot addresses: the invariant that the last slot belonging to a variable has the highest address does not hold. When implemented incorrectly, a loop over an array will immediately terminate if the container spans the end of storage, because the initial position is already greater than the end position. This affects storage array clearing loops generated by both the legacy and the IR code generators. Additionally, in the legacy code generator only, copying operations whose source is an array straddling the end of storage are also affected. At the language level, the buggy code is generated for array assignment, array initialization, the ``delete`` operator, ``<array>.pop()`` and ``<array>.push()``. Note that the compiler inserts a clearing loop not only for the ``delete`` operator, but also to zero storage when overwriting a longer array with a shorter one, popping an element or even pushing an empty element to a dynamic array. The bug is extremely unlikely to be triggered accidentally, because a short dynamic array is practically never allocated right at the storage boundary. From 0.2.0, static layouts are limited to 2**256 slots, so an array can only straddle the end of storage when inline assembly or ``uint512`` slot arithmetic places it there. Inherited from Solidity 0.8.23: upstream SOL-2025-1, fixed in Solidity 0.8.32.
